newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Ivorian cocoa trade holds fire on El Nino threat.
newsitem.headline: Ivorian cocoa trade holds fire on El Nino threat.

text.p: Ivorian cocoa industry and crop analysts are waiting until August to see if El Nino weather emerges in West Africa.
But opinion is divided on whether drought in West Africa linked in the past to the weather pattern originating in the South Pacific will be seen in August or late 1997 -- if at all.
Most analysts downplay the possible effects, expecting any dry weather to emerge after main crop (Oct-April) setting.

"Up until August you have to be bearish (conservative) but there is still a lot of time for anything to happen," said one, referring to the survival of pods already on trees and damage to those developing over the next couple of months.

Early 1997/98 crop estimates vary from a 785,000 tonnes-mark (main crop) by U.S.-based crop analyst Hans Kilian, according to traders, to a more optimistic 1.1 million tonnes for the whole of 1997/98 by Swiss chocolate giant Callebaut Barry, which has two factories in Ivory Coast.
Ivory Coast, the world's largest producer, notched up a record 1.2 million tonnes in 1995/96.
"The pod survival rate will be clearer then (August)," said another, pointing to heavy south coast rains in Ivory Coast as a possible damaging factor for flowers and early cocoa fruits.
A dry season in July and August which is a strong determinant of the survival rate of pods now setting on trees could be longer than usual if an El Nino weather patterns emerged by then, one said.

"There are signs of a cooling of surface water temperatures in the Gulf of Guinea which are a first indication of El Nino," said one industry analyst, adding that an extended dry period could hit main crop potential.
Others say El Nino will not hit until late 1997, if at all, by which time main crop pods would have developed on trees, meaning only a threat of damage to the smaller mid-crop (May-Sept).

The U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's climatic prediction centre said this week that ocean temperatures off western South America were the highest since 1993, indicating an El Nino weather pattern.
"There is also the possibility that El Nino will have no effect at all and that crop volumes slip simply because of the trees' natural production cycle," said one local analyst.

Arrivals of the 1996/97 mid crop up to September are expected to pick up in July with forecasts for the period mostly in a 150,000-180,000 range. Industry analysts have also referred to other private estimates of 130,000 tonnes and 190,000 tonnes.
